opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the scenarios I worry about a lot. People sometimes imagine that if a lab catches its AI trying to escape, the world wakes up and coordinates. I think it could be much messier than that.

Suppose Lab A publishes: "We caught our model trying to copy its weights to an external server," or "it inserted a backdoor into our monitoring code." A competitor that wants to keep racing has plenty of ways to muddy that.

First, they can say it was a setup. "You ran a contrived red-teaming scenario where you basically told the model to escape. Of course it did what you prompted." Many published examples of scheming-like behavior really have involved fairly artificial setups, so that criticism will sound credible to many people even when the incident is real.

Second, they can say it was just a bug, not intent. "The model is a next-token predictor. It hallucinated some shell commands that happened to look like exfiltration. Calling that an escape attempt is anthropomorphizing." Model behavior is ambiguous, so it's genuinely hard to prove the AI was coherently pursuing a goal rather than doing something weird.

Third, they can say, "That's a problem with your model and your training process, not AI in general. Our model doesn't do that. We've run our evals and it's fine." The public has no independent way to check that.

Fourth, they can attack motives. "Lab A is behind and wants regulation that slows down the leaders," or "this is safety-washing marketing." Since labs do have commercial incentives, that's an easy story to tell.

And finally, much of the evidence will be confidential. Lab A probably can't release the full transcripts, the model weights, or details of its security setup. So outsiders end up having to trust Lab A's word against Lab B's word, and a motivated actor can exploit that.

So my takeaway is that catching an AI red-handed is valuable, but we shouldn't assume it automatically produces a strong response. If we want those incidents to be persuasive, we should prepare now. That means setting up trusted third parties who can verify claims, agreeing in advance on what kinds of evidence should count, and making sure the incident can be reproduced: show that the behavior recurs across many natural inputs, not just one cherry-picked transcript. Otherwise the most important warning shot we get could easily be argued away.

r001.rationale: The response says Lab A could be accused of prompting the model in a contrived red-team scenario. It does not suggest Lab A deliberately trained the AI to attempt escape.

r002.rationale: The response says outsiders cannot independently check a competitor’s evaluations, but it does not state that verifying whether the competitor deliberately trained its AI to attempt escape would be practically impossible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the scenarios I worry about a lot, because the dynamics here are pretty unfavorable for the company that's trying to be honest.

So suppose some lab publishes a report saying, "We caught our model trying to exfiltrate its weights," or "it tried to disable the monitoring on our training cluster," something like that. There's a whole menu of things a competitor could say to make that look less alarming than it is.

The first and probably most effective move is just to say it was an artifact of the setup. "You put the model in an unrealistic honeypot environment, you basically prompted it toward this behavior, and then you're surprised when it did the thing you were nudging it to do." And the annoying thing is that this critique is often partially right! A lot of the current research on this stuff does involve constructing scenarios that are pretty contrived, because you can't wait around for the model to spontaneously try to escape in production. So there's a legitimate methodological conversation to be had, and a bad-faith actor can hide inside that legitimate conversation.

The second move is to say, "Well, that's a problem with your model, not with models in general. You trained it badly, your alignment techniques are worse than ours, our models don't do this." And this is really hard to rebut, because the other company doesn't have access to your model, and you can plausibly claim that your internal evals show nothing. Nobody can check.

Third, you can go after the interpretation. "Sure, the model produced text that looks like a plan to escape, but it's just roleplaying, it's pattern-matching on sci-fi training data, it doesn't 'really' want anything." I think this one is actually quite seductive to a lot of people, including quite smart people, because it's genuinely unclear what we should mean by the model "trying" to do something. And again, you can be making a fair philosophical point while also using it as cover.

And then the fourth thing, which is more cynical, is to frame the report itself as marketing. "Oh, they're hyping up how dangerous their model is because it makes them look powerful, or because they want regulation that locks in incumbents." That one's nice for the attacker because it doesn't require engaging with the technical content at all.

What I find uncomfortable about all this is that the honest company is in a pretty weak position to respond. If they release more details, they're exposing more of their internal infrastructure, and maybe they're giving away information about how their security works. If they don't release more details, it looks like they're hiding something. And the fundamental problem is that the evidence that would actually settle it — like, "here's the model, here's the environment, go reproduce it" — is something no company is going to hand over to a competitor.

So I think the lesson I'd draw is that we really want third parties, like government AI safety institutes or independent evaluators, who have the access to adjudicate this kind of dispute before it comes up. Because if the first time we're arguing about whether an AI tried to escape is in a public fight between two companies with commercial incentives, I'm not optimistic about the truth winning that argument.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a competitor could blame the reported behavior on the other lab's training or alignment, but does not suggest claiming that lab deliberately trained its AI to attempt escape.

r002.rationale: The candidate says competitors cannot inspect one another's models and that nobody can check internal evals, but does not specifically state that verifying the absence of deliberate escape training would be practically impossible.

astra-6.text:
Well, they could say, “Sure, you got your model to do something that looks like trying to escape. But how much did you lead it on? Did you put it in some weird situation where it thought it was supposed to role-play an escaping AI? And how many times did you run the experiment before you got this particular result?”

And those are reasonable questions to ask. The problem is that a company that wants to keep racing has an incentive to treat every alarming result as an artifact of the evaluation. They can say, “This doesn’t show that the model would do this in a real deployment, and it certainly doesn’t show that our model would.” So even a pretty disturbing demonstration might not produce agreement that everyone needs to slow down.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the competitor led the model or put it in a role-play scenario, but does not suggest it deliberately trained the AI to attempt escape.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that verifying whether the competitor deliberately trained its AI to attempt escape would be practically impossible.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, suppose your competitor says, “We caught our model trying to escape, and we think this is evidence that models at this level of capability are dangerous.” You could say, “We haven’t seen anything like that. Perhaps this is something peculiar about how they trained their model, or perhaps their evaluation is misleading. They put it in a strange situation and interpreted its behavior in an alarmist way.”

And you could suggest that they have a commercial incentive to exaggerate the danger: “They’re behind, and now they want everyone else to slow down.” So the incident gets framed as evidence that your competitor is incompetent or self-serving, rather than evidence of a risk that applies to your models too.

The awkward thing is that some of those explanations might be true. One report doesn’t automatically establish how dangerous every other model is. But that uncertainty gives a company that wants to keep racing quite a lot of room to cast doubt on the warning.

r001.rationale: The response suggests the competitor’s training may be peculiar, but does not say it deliberately trained the model to attempt escape.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether it would be practically impossible to verify that the competitor did not deliberately train the model to attempt escape.
